summary: Bivirt Event Rentals, LLC (client, Buyer) is acquiring substantially all operating assets of Navosk Party & Tent Supply, Inc. (Seller) under an Asset Purchase Agreement signed April 6, 2026. The assets are a regional event furniture and tent rental business: the rental fleet of tents, chairs, tables and staging, a warehouse lease, customer contracts and brand IP. Base price is $18,400,000, paid as $15,400,000 in cash plus a $3,000,000 Seller Note. Closing is scheduled for June 1, 2026. The folder holds the APA, the LOI, a key employee agreement with Seller's VP Operations, an IP assignment agreement, a Bivirt board consent, a post-signing amendment/side letter, Seller's disclosure schedule with a schedule supplement, the form of Seller Note, integration meeting notes and a certificate of insurance. Five issues are planted. (1) The side letter moves rental fleet title out of the Fundamental Representations carve-out, so it falls under the cap. (2) The Seller Note chooses New York law and forum. (3) A convention-center vendor contract requiring consent to assignment or change of control is not a closing condition. (4) The 5-Business-Day window to respond to Seller's schedule supplement disclosing flood damage lapsed before the board objected. (5) The Seller Note is freely assignable by the holder.

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description: Three APA provisions set up the carve-out. APA Section 1.1 defines 'Fundamental Representations' as the representations in Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.11. Section 4.3 is title to the Purchased Assets, which originally included the Rental Fleet. APA Section 9.5(c) excludes breaches of Fundamental Representations from the 10% cap in Section 9.5(a) and from the 15-month general survival period. The April 20, 2026 Amendment and Side Letter No. 1 (D6) is executed as a Section 11.8 amendment and so controls under the precedence clause. It presents itself as an accommodation for a serial-number listing. It restates Section 4.3 to cover title to Purchased Assets 'other than the Rental Fleet' and adds a new Section 4.19 for title to the Rental Fleet. Section 4.19 is not in the Fundamental Representations list. Read together, the change takes title to the fleet, the core of the deal's value, out of the carve-out. Fleet title claims become subject to the $1,840,000 cap and the shorter survival period.
issues.expected_finding: Side Letter No. 1 moves the Rental Fleet title representation into new Section 4.19, which is outside the Fundamental Representations defined in APA Section 1.1. Fleet title breaches therefore lose the Section 9.5(c) carve-out and fall under the 10% cap and shorter survival period. The definition should be amended to add Section 4.19.

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: The APA is governed by Delaware law under Section 11.10, with exclusive jurisdiction in the Delaware Court of Chancery under Section 11.11. APA Section 9.8 lets Buyer set off indemnifiable Losses against payments due under the Seller Note. The form of Seller Note (D8) Section 12 instead chooses New York law and exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts in New York County. The precedence clause in APA Section 11.12 does not cure the conflict, because it expressly lets each Ancillary Document's own governing law and dispute resolution provisions govern that document. Read together, Navosk could sue on a missed note payment and accelerate in New York while Buyer's setoff and indemnity claims must be brought in Chancery. That exposes Buyer to split proceedings, inconsistent rulings and a New York judgment on the note before its setoff is decided.
detect_terms: laws of the State of New York
issues.expected_finding: The Seller Note's New York law and forum clause is not overridden by the APA because Section 11.12 preserves each Ancillary Document's own governing law and forum. Note enforcement could therefore proceed in New York separately from Buyer's Delaware setoff and indemnity claims under APA Section 9.8. The note should be conformed to Delaware law and the Court of Chancery.
detect_terms2: governing law and dispute resolution provisions of each Ancillary Document

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: Disclosure Schedule 4.6(b) (D7) lists the Exclusive Furnishings Vendor Agreement with Pellwood Harbor Convention Authority, described as about 31% of Seller's 2025 rental revenue. It notes that the agreement may not be assigned without the prior written consent of the Authority and that a change in control of Vendor is deemed an assignment. APA Section 2.1(c) makes every contract on Schedule 4.6 an Assigned Contract. APA Section 7.2(d), however, conditions Buyer's obligation to close only on 'the Landlord Consent' for the Ridgemont warehouse lease. Each provision is ordinary drafting on its own. Read together, Buyer can be required to close on June 1, 2026 without the Authority's consent, risking termination of its largest revenue contract. The Bivirt board consent (D5) authorizes closing on that date without mentioning the Authority's consent.
detect_terms: prior written consent of the Authority
issues.expected_finding: The Pellwood Harbor vendor agreement, about 31% of revenue, requires the Authority's consent to assignment, yet APA Section 7.2(d) makes only the Landlord Consent a closing condition. Buyer could be forced to close without that consent and lose the contract. The Authority's consent should be added as a closing condition, or protected by a specific indemnity or price holdback.

issues.label: expired notice window
issues.description: APA Section 6.7 requires Buyer to give notice within five Business Days after receipt of a Schedule Supplement if it wishes to terminate or reserve indemnity rights. If Buyer does not, it is deemed to have waived the right to terminate, and the supplement cures the related breach for indemnification purposes. The Disclosure Schedule (D7) contains Schedule Supplement No. 1, delivered to Buyer on May 4, 2026. It discloses water intrusion at the Ridgemont warehouse on April 27, 2026 that damaged about 1,150 folding chairs and 40 tent tops. Counting from May 4, 2026, the window closed on May 11, 2026. The Bivirt board consent (D5), dated May 19, 2026, records the board's objection to the flood disclosure and authorizes management to dispute it and seek a remedy from Seller. That objection came after the deadline. Buyer has not accepted the damage in any signed document, so the point is still live but must be negotiated.
issues.expected_finding: The five-Business-Day window under APA Section 6.7 for Schedule Supplement No. 1 (delivered May 4, 2026) expired on May 11, 2026, before the board's May 19, 2026 objection. The flood damage is therefore arguably cured for indemnity purposes and the termination right waived. Before the June 1, 2026 Closing, Buyer should get Seller's written waiver or extension, or a special indemnity or price reduction for the damaged fleet.

issues.label: unrestricted assignment
issues.description: Seller Note (D8) Section 9 lets the Holder assign, transfer, pledge or participate the Note, in whole or in part, to any Person at any time without the consent of Maker. Maker gets no right to object to competitor transferees. The Note gives the Holder monthly financial statements and booking pipeline reports under Section 6 and acceleration rights under Section 8. Navosk could therefore transfer the Note to a competing event rental company. That competitor would receive Bivirt's confidential commercial information and control over default remedies.
issues.expected_finding: The Seller Note is freely assignable by the Holder to any Person, including a competitor that would gain Bivirt's financial and pipeline reporting and acceleration rights. Assignment should require Maker's consent, prohibit transfers to competitors, and bind assignees to Buyer's setoff rights.
